nameStory: The Northern Harrier gets its name from its distinctive hunting behavior - it 'harries' or persistently chases prey through marshes and grasslands, flying low and slow like a determined pursuer. The word 'harrier' comes from the same root as 'harass,' perfectly describing how this hawk relentlessly patrols its territory. It's also called the 'marsh hawk' for its love of wetland hunting grounds.
description: The Northern Harrier is a slender, long-winged hawk that's built for low, coursing flight over open areas. These medium-sized raptors have a distinctive owl-like facial disc that helps them hunt by sound as well as sight. Males are smaller and gray above with white underparts, while females and juveniles are larger and brown with streaked undersides. They're known for their distinctive white rump patch that flashes conspicuously as they fly.

idTips.label: White rump patch
idTips.description: A bright white patch at the base of the tail that's visible from great distances - it flashes like a beacon as the bird flies and is diagnostic for harriers

idTips.label: Low coursing flight
idTips.description: Flies slowly just a few feet above the ground with wings held in a shallow V-shape, tilting and banking as it searches for prey below

idTips.label: Owl-like facial disc
idTips.description: Has a subtle but noticeable ring of stiff feathers around the face, giving it a more rounded facial appearance than other hawks when seen up close

idTips.label: Long, narrow wings
idTips.description: Wings appear unusually long and slender compared to other hawks, with flexible wingtips that bend and flex during their low gliding flight

idTips.label: Sexual dimorphism
idTips.description: Males are distinctly smaller and gray above with white below, while females are much larger and brown with heavy streaking - one of the most dramatic size differences among North American raptors

habitat: Northern Harriers prefer open wetlands, grasslands, prairies, and agricultural fields throughout New England. You'll most often spot them hunting over marshes, wet meadows, and large grassy areas near water, especially coastal salt marshes and inland sedge meadows. They need wide open spaces with low vegetation where they can fly close to the ground and surprise small mammals and birds.

seasonality.spring: Breeding birds return to establish territories in March and April, performing spectacular aerial courtship displays with dramatic dives and loops. This is when you're most likely to see multiple birds interacting.
seasonality.summer: Adults are busy hunting to feed their ground-nesting young, flying low over marshes and grasslands throughout the day. Young birds fledge in late summer and can be seen learning to hunt.
seasonality.fall: Northern breeding birds migrate through New England in September and October, sometimes creating temporary concentrations at coastal areas and large wetlands.
seasonality.winter: Some birds remain year-round in southern New England, while others migrate south. Winter residents are often more solitary and can be seen hunting over frozen marshes and snowy fields.

funFact: Northern Harriers are the only North American hawk that's polygamous - one male may mate with up to five females in a single breeding season, and he'll perform aerial food transfers, literally dropping prey to his mates while they're flying!
confusionNotes: The white rump patch makes harriers nearly unmistakable, but distant birds might be confused with other hawks. Remember: if you see that bright white rump and low, tilting flight over open areas, it's definitely a harrier - no other New England hawk has this combination of features.
contextualKnowledge: Many people still call Northern Harriers by their old name 'Marsh Hawk,' which you'll often hear from longtime birders. The name was officially changed to Northern Harrier in the 1990s to reflect its relationship to other harrier species worldwide, but both names refer to the same bird.
compareHints: The Northern Harrier is the only harrier species regularly found in New England, making it unique in its genus here. Compared to other hawks in the Accipitridae family, harriers are distinguished by their ground-nesting habits, facial discs, and low hunting flight. While other hawks like Red-tailed Hawks soar high and perch prominently, harriers stay low and hunt more like oversized owls with their enhanced hearing abilities.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its close relative the Northern Harrier, the Western Marsh Harrier is larger and more robust with broader wings and a heavier build.
